extracted.intended_audience: Applicants seeking registration to practice before the USPTO (prospective patent practitioners), OED staff, and legal counsel advising such applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules governing review of applications to register and practice before the USPTO in patent cases, focusing on required moral character/reputation, rehabilitation evidence, waiver of regulatory waiting periods, and procedural limits on petitions for review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good moral character and reputation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director of the USPTO requires agents, attorneys, or other persons to show that they are of good moral character and reputation prior to registration (35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D); 37 C.F.R. § 11.7(a)(2)(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The OED Director investigates applicants' moral character and reputation and may deny registration where an applicant fails to demonstrate he presently possesses the requisite good moral character and reputation. Failure to meet this requirement is a sufficient basis for denial of an application for registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof on applicant to establish rehabilitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant bears the burden of establishing rehabilitation and present good moral character to the satisfaction of the OED Director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An applicant must affirmatively demonstrate rehabilitation; mere assertions or minimal compliance are insufficient. The decision emphasizes that 'Petitioner has the burden of establishing rehabilitation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehabilitation standard: affirmative, prolonged demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: Rehabilitation requires an affirmative demonstration over a prolonged period of sincere regret and rehabilitative conduct (citing prior OED decisions and case law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is 'not enough that petitioner kept out of trouble while being watched on probation; he must affirmatively demonstrate over a prolonged period his sincere regret and rehabilitation.' Case citations stress that simply serving the sentence and not reoffending does not prove rehabilitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community service and achievements as relevant but not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Community service and personal achievements are relevant factors in evaluating rehabilitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such activities may support a claim of rehabilitation but minimal compliance with sentencing terms or only doing the minimum required does not suffice to establish the trustworthiness necessary for practice before the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-year waiting period after completion of sentence or probation
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory rule requiring a waiting period: applicants convicted of a misdemeanor involving moral turpitude or interference with the administration of justice generally must wait two years after completion of sentence or probation before reapplying (37 C.F.R. § 11.7(h)(1)(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two-year delay is a codified policy to allow time to accumulate a record of positive action and maintain public confidence in registered practitioners. The decision applies the waiting period to the petitioner and calculates the reapplication eligibility date accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary-circumstances waiver standard (37 C.F.R. § 11.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Waiver of the two-year waiting period is permissible only upon a showing of 'extraordinary circumstances' under 37 C.F.R. § 11.3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision explains that examples of extraordinary circumstances are narrow (e.g., conviction overturned) and that evidence such as early termination of probation, divorce-related stress, compliance with probation, or focus on career generally do not amount to the extraordinary situation contemplated by the regulation. The petitioner must show circumstances sufficiently exceptional to justify suspension of the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: New evidence not considered on petition for review
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition to the USPTO Director for review of an OED final decision must be limited to the facts of record; the Director will consider no new evidence (37 C.F.R. § 11.2(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence submitted after the OED Director's final decision (e.g., letters, sentence modification orders, transcripts) will not be considered in the Director's review. Such new evidence may be filed, but it is not part of the review record under the regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of sentence modification and retained probation conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A court's modification of sentence that retains probation conditions (travel reporting, protective orders, etc.) does not necessarily establish rehabilitation and may weigh against a finding of present good moral character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a judge maintains probation conditions despite modifying a sentence, those conditions support the conclusion that rehabilitation has not been fully demonstrated for purposes of professional registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct underlying convictions relevant to moral-character assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature of the underlying misconduct (e.g., interference with administration of justice, resisting arrest, violations of protective or pendente lite orders) is relevant to assessing moral character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision notes that actions taken during domestic disputes (e.g., violating orders, fleeing police) are not the sort of circumstances that justify altering normal moral-character standards; such conduct can support a denial of registration absent strong rehabilitative evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy justification: protecting public confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory standards (including the two-year waiting period) serve to maintain public confidence in persons registered to practice before the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision explicitly states that following the rule 'serves to maintain public confidence' and that justice is served by applying the waiting period to allow reestablishment of reputation and moral character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural role of OED and appeal route
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) receives and acts on registration applications, conducts investigations, and issues final decisions; an individual dissatisfied with an OED final decision may petition the USPTO Director limited to the record (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.2(b)(2)-(b)(3), 11.2(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets out the procedural framework: OED fact-finding and decisions, followed by limited review by the Director (no new evidence), and the availability (subject to regulatory limits) of requests for waiver under § 11.3 or reapplication after the waiting period.
